title: Nat Narain

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Ramkali, and your line was the richest raga. Which Ramkali shabad did you find, and what line stayed with you? Day one thousand one hundred two.

At a wedding, the dhol player picks up the pace, and before anyone decides to, feet are moving under the tables. Some music simply won't let a body sit still. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga this path describes in that key. It's a short section, tucked in after the long, calm rooms of Ramkali, and its name is Nat Narain. Yesterday's raga was deep and roomy. Today's is small and quick. So what does a lively raga do with devotion? Today, Nat Narain.
screen: `FEET MOVING UNDER THE TABLES.` → `AFTER RAMKALI, A SMALL ROOM.` → `NAT NARAIN.`

segments.voice: Narain is a name for God, and here it is part of a raga's name, and the hymns gathered under it belong to Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, and Guru Arjan, the fifth. The section opens with Guru Ram Das talking to his own mind. Given here in plain English, not word for word: my mind, repeat the Lord's Name day and night, and countless wrongs are set aside. Notice who the speaker is talking to. He isn't lecturing a crowd. He's turning to himself, the way you'd turn to a friend who keeps drifting off mid-conversation. That habit runs all through Gurbani: the mind gets spoken to directly, coaxed, encouraged, sometimes scolded. In a lively raga, the coaxing has a bounce in its step. Step back and the pattern shows. The Granth gives devotion many moods, a raga for each, and one of those moods is lively. The same Name that is sung slow and heavy in one section comes back quick and bright in another. The Granth doesn't set one speed for loving God. The raga sets the color; the Name stays the same. And the liveliness isn't decoration. In kirtan, the music is there to carry the words, not to cover them. A bright tune that buries the hymn has missed the point. A bright tune that gets a tired mind back on its feet has found it. So today's raga is short, quick and friendly: a Guru turning to his own mind and saying, again, day and night. That's today's line: lively.
screen: `NARAIN: A NAME FOR GOD.` · `MY MIND, REPEAT THE NAME.` · `DEVOTION HAS MANY MOODS.` · `THE TUNE CARRIES THE WORDS.` · then, large: `LIVELY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a lively start, then a steady sit. Sit up tall. For a few breaths, breathe a little brisker than usual, not hard, just the way you'd breathe walking up a short hill. If brisk breathing doesn't suit you, skip straight to the next part. Then let the breath settle back to its own pace and stay with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each out-breath, the way Guru Ram Das turns to his mind: again, and again. If you don't, count your out-breaths up to ten and begin again. Later today, find one Nat Narain shabad and listen to it once, all the way through. The bell holds the time.
Nat Narain. A short, lively raga of the Guru Granth Sahib, where Guru Ram Das turns to his own mind and says: repeat the Name, day and night. Today's word.
Your line: lively. Once today, when your attention drags, talk to your own mind the way the hymn does, kindly and directly: come on, once more. Day one thousand one hundred two.

howItsDone: In kirtan, Sikh musicians sing the shabads of the Nat Narain section in that raga; the raga named at the head of a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib gives the musical color it is sung in.
